short: The king who made Sweden a great power and reworked European battlefield tactics.
full:
Gustav II Adolf came to the throne in 1611, aged sixteen, with wars against Denmark, Russia and Poland already running. He settled them in turn, taking Ingria and Kexholm from Russia in 1617 and Livonia from Poland by 1629, then landed in Pomerania in 1630 to intervene in the German war on the Protestant side.

His reputation rests on reform as much as conquest. He standardised his artillery around light regimental guns that moved with the infantry, thinned his formations to six ranks so that more muskets could fire at once, and combined massed salvo fire with cavalry that charged home with the sword rather than trotting up to fire pistols. Parish conscription gave him a national core, though by 1632 most of his troops were German hirelings. He was killed at Lützen in November 1632, sixteen months after his victory at Breitenfeld, and left Sweden committed to a war it fought for another sixteen years. Sabaton's "The Lion from the North" takes his German campaign as its subject.
